segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Law

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the great novels in the English language.
Over this series, we're going to take Dickens apart — sentence by sentence, image by image — and ask what makes this extraordinary book tick.
Today we begin at the beginning: the fog, the mud, and the Court of Chancery.
Three extraordinary minds are joining me today, and I want to introduce them properly.
First, Dr. Eleanor Hartley — novelist, teacher of creative writing, and one of the most acute readers of Dickens's craft I know.
Eleanor has a rare gift: she makes the architecture of fiction feel thrilling, not clinical.
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us — retired Oxford don, lifelong reader of Dickens as a moralist, and a man whose prose style alone is worth the admission price.
Edmund reads Bleak House as a novel about character — about goodness, weakness, and the testing of individual souls.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive.
Oliver hears what the rest of us only read — the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments Dickens wrote for the voice.
Now — Chapter One. Dickens gives us no gentle entry into this world.
Oliver, you've read this opening aloud more times than any of us. What happens when you first encounter that word — just 'London'?
That single word — 'London' — is one of the great opening gestures in fiction.
Dickens doesn't say 'It was a dark and stormy night' — he doesn't give you a sentence at all.
He gives you a noun. A place. A verdict.
And then he just starts accumulating — mud, fog, slipping passengers, miserable horses — before he drops this on you.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur. Up Holborn Hill. On a Tuesday morning in November.
It's preposterously funny, and it's deadly serious — because if London looks like the world before Creation, what hope does it have?
And notice the grammar of that passage, which is doing something extremely strange.
Those opening sentences have no main verbs. 'London. Implacable November weather. Smoke lowering down.'
They're noun phrases, fragments — as if the language itself can't quite form complete thoughts in this fog.
The style enacts the content. The syntax is foggy.
And then there's that extraordinary phrase — 'gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun.'
"Gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
'The death of the sun' — that's not satire anymore, that's elegy. That's apocalypse.
Dickens holds those two registers simultaneously — the comic grotesque and the genuinely terrible — and that tension is what makes the novel so vertiginous.
I take the point about register — it's well observed — but I'd resist the impulse to reach immediately for allegory.
This fog is, first and foremost, a literary atmosphere — magnificently rendered, but still an atmosphere.
What Dickens is establishing is a moral climate — the sense that confusion and obscurity have settled over human affairs like weather.
And then he locates that confusion precisely — in Chancery, in the law — and that is where Dickens becomes truly formidable.
He writes — and this is the passage I return to again and again —

"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds this day in the sight of heaven and earth."
'Most pestilent of hoary sinners' — that is the language of the pulpit. That is Dickens as moral preacher.
He is not merely describing an institution — he is delivering a judgement, in the oldest sense of that word.
Edmund is right that it's the language of the pulpit — but what strikes me performing it is how the rhetoric builds.
Dickens does something almost musical in the great Chancery passage — that repeated 'which has its...' construction.
Listen to it — it's an anaphora, like a terrible litany:

"This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance."
Every clause adds a new victim — the landowner, the lunatic, the dead, the beggar — the indictment keeps widening.
And it ends — and this is the masterstroke — not with Dickens's own fury but with the warning of Chancery's own practitioners.
'Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here.' The lawyers themselves say this.
That ending is devastating precisely because Dickens doesn't claim it — he attributes it.
He's been raging for paragraphs, and then he steps back and says — don't take my word for it.
Ask any honourable man who practises there. They'll tell you themselves.
It's a brilliant rhetorical pivot — and it also sets up the entire novel's moral architecture.
Because Jarndyce and Jarndyce is not going to be solved. The fog is not going to lift.
The only question is what kind of person you become while you wait for a justice that never arrives.
Now there I think Eleanor has put her finger on precisely the right question — and it is, at bottom, a moral one.
The fog and the court are the given conditions of the novel. They cannot be reformed within the pages of a fiction.
What can be done — what Dickens shows us across eight hundred pages — is that individual human beings may choose how to conduct themselves within those conditions.
Esther Summerson does not wait for Chancery to become just. She becomes good. That distinction matters enormously.
And that tension — between systemic critique and individual character — is exactly what we'll be tracing through this whole series.
We've established the fog, we've felt the weight of that Chancery indictment, and we've glimpsed the moral stakes Dickens is setting.
In our next segment, we'll meet the inhabitants of this fog-bound world — and ask how Dickens introduces character in a novel of this scale and ambition.

segments.title: Deep Dive: Richard's Slow Burn—Ambition into Ruin

utterances.text: We turn now to one of Dickens's most devastating portrait studies — Richard Carstone.
Young, gifted, charming — and ground to nothing by Chancery and his own nature.
Sir Edmund Leigh has been waiting, I think, for precisely this conversation.
Edmund reads Richard not as a victim of an unjust system, but as a character study in the failure of will — which makes him, if anything, more tragic.
Richard Carstone is, for me, among the most finely observed young men in all of English fiction.
And Dickens is merciless with him — merciless in the way that genuine compassion sometimes requires.
The diagnosis is delivered early, and it is exact.
Esther observes that the educational system had allowed him to dash through his tasks with fair credit and distinction —
"in a fitful, dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train."
Fitful. Dazzling. Two words that contain the whole of Richard's tragedy.
And then the great paradox — Dickens frames it as a classical inversion, almost Aristotelian in its precision.
His gifts, Esther tells us, were like fire and water —
"though excellent servants, they were very bad masters."
There is an almost Johnsonian economy to that formulation — it belongs in a book of maxims.
What strikes me about that passage is the structural cunning of it.
Esther is narrating, which means we're getting this diagnosis filtered through someone who loves Richard — someone who cannot be entirely objective.
And yet her judgment is absolute. Dickens uses Esther's warmth as a kind of credential — her affection makes the verdict harder to dispute.
The dual-narrator structure is doing exactly what it was designed to do — Esther's intimacy here prevents the reader from dismissing this as authorial moralising.
And the image of fire and water — Edmund is right that it has a proverbial weight.
But it also does something more — it makes Richard's qualities sound magnificent, even as it condemns their misuse.
Precisely so — and that is what separates Dickens from the reformist pamphleteer he is sometimes reduced to being.
He does not present Richard as a victim of Chancery alone. The suit is the occasion, not the cause.
The cause is in Richard himself — in that fitful, dazzling reliance on native brilliance never disciplined into application.
Any number of young men have faced Chancery and survived it.
Richard is destroyed because he cannot resist the suit's terrible gravity — he throws himself into it as into a vocation.
He tells us so, with terrible self-awareness —
"I devote myself to it. I make it the object of my life."
The dreadful irony is that this is perhaps the most committed Richard has ever been to anything.
You know what strikes me every time I perform that speech? The rhythm of it.
"I am young and earnest, and energy and determination have done wonders many a time."
That's a young man convincing himself in real time. Dickens writes it as a kind of desperate crescendo.
On the page you can analyse the irony at leisure. In performance, you feel the character's heartbeat.
And then — this is the cruelty of it — Dickens turns the omniscient narrator loose on Richard in Chapter 39.
The third-person voice steps in when Esther's affection would soften the blow too much.
And it delivers this — almost like a prosecuting counsel summing up —
"injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat."
Jarndyce — good, decent, self-sacrificing Jarndyce — becomes the enemy because Richard needs something solid to hate.
That switch to the omniscient narrator is a masterstroke of structural economy.
Esther cannot narrate Richard's corruption of Jarndyce's reputation without implicating herself — she loves both men.
So Dickens steps back, cold-eyed, and gives us the mechanism — the psychology of displacement laid bare.
What's remarkable is how modern it feels — this is almost a clinical description of how resentment finds its object.
And then Richard himself gives it to us in his own voice, devastatingly, to Woodcourt.
He says — and there is something almost noble in the candour —
"I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else."
He knows. He has always known. And knowing has not saved him.
That passage to Woodcourt is, for me, the moral centre of Richard's story.
He has not lost his conscience. He has simply surrendered his will to something larger than himself.
And listen to the syntax of the final capitulation —
"I have an object now — or it has me."
That parenthetical correction — "or it has me" — is one of the most quietly terrible things Dickens ever wrote.
Richard amends his own sentence in the act of speaking it, and in doing so delivers his own verdict.
That dash — that pause before "or it has me" — is a performance gift wrapped in prose.
I've performed that line perhaps sixty times, and the silence before the correction never loses its effect.
The audience always catches it — that moment when Richard hears his own untruth and cannot let it stand.
And then Esther watches him — just watches — and what she sees in his face is worse than anything he has said.
Dickens gives us this image of Richard's forced hopefulness —
"it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so conscious of being forced and unsustainable."
"Fierce in its determination to be it." That's not a man hoping. That's a man performing hope for his own benefit.
"Fierce in its determination to be it" — that's Dickens at his most precise, and his most devastating.
The reflexive quality of it — hope straining to look like hope — is a kind of psychological double-bind.
And Esther adds the final cruelty: that even if Chancery had resolved in Richard's favour at that very moment, the marks would have remained.
"The traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach, and disappointment... would have remained upon his features to the hour of his death."
The damage is not contingent on the outcome. That is a genuinely tragic vision.
And the novel's final image of Richard — before his death, in Esther's account — confirms it with absolute finality.
Dickens does not show us a villain, nor a victim. He shows us a ruin.
Esther observes him — thin, languid, slovenly — with those large bright eyes gone dull and restless.
And Dickens reaches for a formulation that is, I think, among his most memorable —
"There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away."
A ruin of youth which is not like age. It is a distinction that cuts to the bone.
Age is natural. This is waste. And Dickens will not let us miss the difference.
I've never found a way to read that line without a silence after it.
Any commentary feels redundant. Dickens has said the thing completely.
The novel earns its silences. Richard's death, when it comes, will be almost quiet — which is its own kind of devastation.
A ruin of youth which is not like age — we'll carry that line with us.
We've traced the arc from that early educational diagnosis through to the final physical ruin — a complete portrait.
Coming up, we turn to the fog itself — Dickens's great governing image — and what it means to build an entire novel around a single pervasive metaphor.

segments.title: The Law's Machinery: Jo's Silent Witness

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' most ambitious novel and opens it up — chapter by chapter, image by image, sentence by sentence.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's most devastating threads: the boy called Jo.
Jo is a crossing-sweeper — a child of the London streets who knows nothing, owns nothing, and is perpetually told to move on.
He is also, Dickens insists with gathering fury, the novel's sharpest indictment of Victorian England.
Joining me today are three readers who bring very different eyes to this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher whose gift is for the architecture of Dickens' prose — the way a single structural choice can carry an entire chapter's moral weight.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose readings of Dickens remain, for many of us, the gold standard — and who will, I suspect, offer a useful corrective to any reading that turns Jo into pure polemic.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens for audio than almost anyone alive — he hears these passages in his bones, and he'll read them for us today with the ear of a performer.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with that extraordinary passage in Chapter Sixteen, where Dickens inhabits Jo's perspective directly.
What strikes me first about that passage is its grammar — because Dickens makes a radical formal choice right at the start.
He shifts to the infinitive: not 'Jo shuffles' but 'to shuffle,' 'to see,' 'to be.'
It's a grammar of the unrealised — of a life that has never quite arrived at full existence.
And then Dickens takes the most extraordinary step: he shifts into the first person.
The narrator says — and I want Oliver to read this, because it needs to be heard:
"It must be a strange state, not merely to be told that I am scarcely human — as in the case of my offering myself for a witness — but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life!"
That pronoun — 'I' — is everything.
Dickens doesn't describe Jo from the outside; he briefly, shockingly, becomes him.
The narrator colonises Jo's subjectivity at precisely the moment the legal system has declared that subjectivity worthless.
Jo cannot testify in court because he doesn't understand the oath.
So the novel itself becomes his testimony.
I think Eleanor is right about the formal daring, and I don't wish to seem obstructive about the social dimension.
But what moves me about Jo is not primarily his representative function — not what he stands for — but what he actually is.
He is a particular child, with a particular loyalty — to the one man who was kind to him.
Dickens understood — as Dr. Johnson understood — that it is individuals, not abstractions, who command our deepest feeling.
There is a passage in Chapter Eleven that rather proves my point.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That is not polemic.
That is grace — in the oldest sense of the word.
Jo loves the dead man not because the dead man was respectable or religious or deserving, but because he was kind.
Dickens has located something irreducible in human nature, and he has put it in the mouth of a child who cannot even spell his own name.
Edmund, that's beautifully put, and I don't disagree — but speaking as someone who has read those words aloud more times than I can count, I'd add something about the dialect itself.
'He wos wery good to me, he wos' — the repetition at the end, that second 'he wos,' is heartbreaking precisely because it's unnecessary.
Jo has said what he needed to say, and then he says it again — because there's nothing else to say, and because he cannot quite bring himself to stop saying it.
That is Dickens writing for the speaking voice, absolutely and precisely.
And then in Chapter Forty-Six we hear Jo speaking at length for himself — and the dialect does something extraordinary there too.
Let me read a little of it:
"I've been a-chivied and a-chivied, fust by one on you and nixt by another on you, till I'm worritted to skins and bones."
'Chivied' — harassed, hounded — and 'worritted to skins and bones.'
The syntax is fractured, the grammar barely holds — and that is the point.
This is a voice the legal system declared inadmissible, and Dickens is making you hear why that declaration is obscene.
And it builds, doesn't it — across the novel.
By Chapter Nineteen, Dickens has dropped all pretence of neutral observation.
The narrator is addressing Jo directly — but also addressing the reader, and beyond the reader, the Parliament.
The rhetoric becomes savage — but carefully, precisely savage.
Oliver, would you?
"Do you hear, Jo? It is nothing to you or to any one else that the great lights of the parliamentary sky have failed for some few years in this business to set you the example of moving on."
"The one grand recipe remains for you — the profound philosophical prescription — the be-all and the end-all of your strange existence upon earth. Move on!"
'The profound philosophical prescription' — that is withering.
Dickens is mocking the language of governance — the grand, abstract, self-important language — and setting it against the brutal simplicity of what it actually means for Jo.
Move on.
I confess I find that passage somewhat less satisfying than Eleanor does — not because the anger isn't just, but because Dickens here addresses an abstraction rather than a person.
The Parliament is a very large target.
Where the novel reaches its true moral summit, for me, is at Jo's death in Chapter Forty-Seven.
There, Dickens abandons irony altogether and writes what I can only call a lamentation.
The great passage reads as follows:
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order."
"Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
'Wrong reverends' — that small, precise adjective — is the only irony he permits himself.
The rest is pure, unadorned address — almost liturgical.
And that last sentence — 'And dying thus around us every day' — is, I think, among the most devastating in the English novel.
Edmund, I think that's exactly right, and it answers something I've been trying to articulate.
The anaphora — 'Dead, your Majesty, Dead, my lords' — is structurally identical to a legal roll-call.
Dickens is using the form of official address — the very form that excluded Jo — and filling it with the one word the law refused to speak plainly about Jo's life.
Dead.
The novel's entire legal machinery — all that fog, all those Chancery proceedings — has produced one outcome for Jo.
And Dickens names it with one word, seven times.
I have read that passage in recording studios, in theatres, at literary festivals.
The difficulty is always the same: not to ornament it.
Every instinct as a performer tells you to colour each 'Dead,' to make them different — sorrowful here, angry there.
But Dickens has written them identically for a reason.
The sameness is the point.
Dead is dead, whoever you address it to — your Majesty or Jo — and the word does not change its weight.
That's a remarkable place to pause — with the word that Dickens refuses to soften.
In our next segment, we'll follow the fog — Dickens' great opening image — and ask what it actually means when a novelist turns weather into argument.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Mystery and Disguise: Lady Dedlock's Concealment

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' vast, magnificent novel apart scene by scene — and tries to understand how it works.
Today we're entering what I think is the novel's most sustained exercise in psychological suspense: the story of Lady Dedlock and her secret.
From her first appearance in Lincolnshire, something is wrong with her — beautifully, fatally wrong.
To help us unpack that wrongness, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of this novel.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who has spent years studying how Dickens builds his effects from the ground up — the architecture of sentences, the weight of a single image.
Eleanor, your eye for craft is exactly what Lady Dedlock's portrait demands.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a novel about individual character tested by circumstance — about the moral weight each person carries, or fails to carry.
Edmund, Lady Dedlock is nothing if not a character tested almost beyond endurance.
And Oliver Trevelyan has performed more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears the rhythms, the timing, the moments written for the voice.
Oliver, I suspect you've read Lady Dedlock's doom aloud more times than you care to count.
Let's begin at the beginning — with that first extraordinary glimpse of her in Lincolnshire.
What strikes me every time about the Lincolnshire opening is that Dickens gives us the landscape before he gives us the woman — and the landscape is doing all the psychological work.
We get this relentless, almost hypnotic accumulation of wetness and decay before Lady Dedlock appears at all.
Listen to the rhythm of it — Dickens writes:
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
Lead-coloured and Indian ink — those are painting terms, and the repetition of 'view' is doing something very precise.
The world Lady Dedlock inhabits is not merely gloomy — it is rendered in the language of art, of surface, of carefully composed appearance.

And then, at the very end of that long, saturated paragraph, comes the single crack in the facade: she sees a child, a mother, a man coming through the gate — a family — and she is 'put quite out of temper.'
Bored to death, she says — but that particular scene, of all scenes, is what undoes her composure.
And what's so brilliant about it performatively is the gap between what Dickens tells us and what he lets us infer.
She's 'bored to death' — that's her phrase, her social armour, the thing she says about everything.
But a child running to its father through the rain has broken through every layer of it.
When I read this passage aloud, I always take that final sentence very slowly.
Because it's written as comedy — 'bored to death,' the fashionable lady inconvenienced — but the joke is hollow, and the hollowness is the point.
Dickens is doing something an actor dreams of: he's written the subtext into the text without ever naming it.
What Oliver describes so vividly is what I would call the great moral burden Dickens places on this woman from the very first page.
Lady Dedlock has constructed an entire existence around concealment — and that construction has cost her everything that makes life worth living.
The fashion, the boredom, the insolence — these are not character traits. They are the daily price of the secret.
One thinks of Burke on the nature of a life lived in perpetual disguise — that the effort of sustaining a false self consumes all the energy that might otherwise animate a true one.
Lady Dedlock is not bored. She is exhausted by the ceaseless labour of being someone she is not.
Edmund's point about exhaustion leads directly, I think, to that extraordinary phrase Dickens uses repeatedly for her: 'exhausted deity.'
It appears again when she and Tulkinghorn circle each other at Chesney Wold, and the passage is one of the great set-pieces of the whole novel.
Dickens writes, and this is a long quote but every word deserves its place:
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
'Presiding at her own shrine' — she is both the worshipped object and the presiding priestess, which means she is trapped inside her own performance.
And then comes Tulkinghorn — 'the speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.'
That paradox — out of place, yet at home — is the structural key to his menace: he belongs everywhere he shouldn't, and nowhere he should.
I've read Tulkinghorn's lines in — I won't say how many recordings — and what I keep discovering is that Dickens gives him almost nothing to say directly.
He is defined by what he withholds. He is the 'speechless repository' — silence is his instrument of power.
And then the passage builds to that stunning closing sentence — let me read it because it really must be heard:

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
'All this is hidden, for the time' — that 'for the time' is the blade in the velvet.
Dickens has just told you that the concealment is temporary. The revelation is already moving towards them, inexorable.
And somehow that makes you fear for her — not despise her, but fear for her — which is a remarkable emotional achievement.
Oliver is right to note the sympathy Dickens engineers — and I think it is engineered rather deliberately, which is itself interesting.
By rights, Lady Dedlock has committed a deception of the gravest kind against a husband who has given her everything.
Sir Leicester is not a figure of fun in these passages — he is a man of genuine dignity, deceived through no fault of his own.
And yet Dickens never allows us to convert our moral judgement into cold disapproval.
He keeps insisting on her suffering — the cost she has already paid, the cost she continues to pay with every composed and insolent movement.
It is, in the deepest sense, a Christian moral imagination: she is a sinner, but her punishment is already underway from within.
That tension — between the sinner and the sufferer — is precisely what the novel sustains all the way to its catastrophe.
And the collapse, when it comes, arrives in one of the most compressed and terrible sentences in the whole book.
That moment in chapter forty, before the catastrophe is even named — Dickens stages it with an almost unbearable visual economy.
It's just two sentences — the whole revelation takes two sentences — and they work entirely through the contrast of light sources.
Dickens writes:
"By the light of the fire he can be seen looking towards the moonlight. By the moonlight, Lady Dedlock can be seen in profile, perfectly still."
Fire and moonlight — warmth and cold, action and stasis, the lawyer moving and the lady arrested.
'Perfectly still' — those two words are doing the work of a whole chapter of interiority. She has heard everything. She cannot move.
Dickens trusts the image absolutely. He doesn't explain. He doesn't intrude. He just holds the shot.
In performance, that passage requires something close to silence.
You read 'perfectly still' and then you do not rush. You let the listener understand what that stillness costs her.
And then the whole novel lurches forward — because from that moment she is not merely concealing a secret. She is running from its consequences.
The final stage of that flight brings us to chapter fifty-five and one of the most devastating sentences Dickens ever wrote.
"All is broken down. Her name is in these many mouths, her husband knows his wrongs, her shame will be published—may be spreading while she thinks about it."
'May be spreading while she thinks about it' — the present tense, the passive helplessness of it, is almost physical.
It's the feeling of watching something terrible happen and being unable to stop it even in your own mind.
The word that arrests me in that passage is 'wrongs.'
'Her husband knows his wrongs' — not 'her secret,' not 'the truth.' His wrongs.
Dickens is making a legal and moral claim in a single word: Sir Leicester has been wronged, and that wrong is now legible.
And yet — and this is where Dickens' moral imagination exceeds anything doctrinaire — Sir Leicester's response will be one of the most magnanimous acts in Victorian fiction.
The novel does not punish Lady Dedlock through her husband. It offers her, too late, the one thing she never allowed herself: forgiveness.
But before that forgiveness can reach her — and it cannot reach her — there is the final passage, which I find almost unbearable to analyse because it's so perfectly made.
Dickens writes of her final state:

"Thus, a terrible impression steals upon and overshadows her that from this pursuer, living or dead—obdurate and imperturbable before her in his well-remembered shape, or not more obdurate and imperturbable in his coffin-bed—there is no escape but in death."
'Obdurate and imperturbable in his coffin-bed' — Tulkinghorn, now dead, is still implacable.
Death has not released her from him. He pursues her from beyond it.
And then that final clause: 'her strength of self-reliance is overturned and whirled away like a leaf before a mighty wind.'
That 'strength of self-reliance' — that is everything she has been for the entire novel. And it goes like a leaf.
'Whirled away like a leaf before a mighty wind' — Dickens almost never reaches for that register of the sublime, and when he does it always earns it.
He's spent forty chapters building this woman's armour — layer by layer, scene by scene — precisely so he can show us what it looks like when it shatters.
And 'Hunted, she flies' — three words, like a hammer. Short, Anglo-Saxon, final.
After all the elaborate Latinate architecture of the novel's great sentences, those three words are like stepping out of a cathedral into cold air.
I would only add that what makes this passage morally serious, rather than merely pathetic, is that single word 'remorse.'
Dickens writes of 'the complication of her shame, her dread, remorse, and misery.'
Shame and dread we understand — they are consequences visited upon her from without.
But remorse is hers alone — it is the interior judgment she passes on herself, independent of Tulkinghorn, of society, of anyone.
In placing remorse at the centre of her collapse, Dickens refuses to let her be simply a victim of circumstance. She knows what she has done. And that knowledge is the truest part of her doom.
Remorse at the centre of collapse — that is a beautiful and precise place to pause.

We've traced Lady Dedlock from that first cold window in Lincolnshire all the way to the leaf in the mighty wind — and I think what this conversation has shown is how much Dickens trusts image and rhythm to carry what lesser novelists would have to explain.
Eleanor, Edmund, Oliver — thank you.
We'll return in our next segment to the figure who watches all of this from a very different angle: Esther Summerson, and what her narration chooses — and chooses not — to see.

segments.title: Bleak House Comedy: Absurdity and Darkness

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're turning to something that makes Dickens unlike any other Victorian novelist: his comedy.
Not the warm, reassuring comedy of resolution, but something stranger and darker — satire with teeth, absurdity that draws blood.
With me today are three people who know this novel with unusual intimacy.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley, who teaches creative writing and has spent years studying how Dickens builds his effects from the sentence upward.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, who reads Bleak House as a great moral novel first and a social document second.
And Oliver Trevelyan, the actor and writer who has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — and who hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Let's begin with Harold Skimpole — one of the most unsettling comic creations in all of English fiction.
Skimpole is the novel's great guilty pleasure.
He's designed to be charming, and he is charming — which is precisely what makes him monstrous.
There's a passage in chapter thirty-one where he does something almost incomprehensible with the figure of Jo — and he does it with such elegance that you nearly let him get away with it.
He says — and I want to read this properly because the rhythm is everything —

"Society, which has taken upon itself the general arrangement of the whole system of spoons and professes to have a spoon for our young friend, does NOT produce that spoon; and our young friend, therefore, says 'You really must excuse me if I seize it.'"
The spoon metaphor is so perfectly ludicrous that for a moment you're laughing — and then you remember Jo is a starving child.
Dickens gives Skimpole the wit to make poverty sound almost aesthetically interesting, and then expects us to feel the obscenity of that.
What you're describing is what I'd call the novel's most dangerous structural trick.
Dickens is using Skimpole to do something that the novel — at its earnest, social-reforming level — absolutely cannot do directly.
He can't have his omniscient narrator make poverty sound poetic, because that would be monstrous.
So he creates a character who will do it instead — and then he makes sure we despise that character for doing it.
It's a kind of moral ventriloquism.
And look at the prose rhythm of Skimpole's speech — it's all qualified clauses and elegant pivots, the syntax of someone who will always find a way to make his self-interest sound reasonable.
I won't quarrel with any of that.
But I think one sometimes overstates the sociological and understates the moral in Skimpole.
Dickens' real target is not society's failure to produce spoons — it is Skimpole's failure of conscience.
The spoon speech works as satire, yes — but what it exposes is a man who has cultivated irresponsibility into an art form.
Burke would have recognised the type: the man of sensibility who has exempted himself from the duties of sympathy.
Dickens was a moralist before he was a reformer, and the comedy here is fundamentally a comedy of character — of a soul in a very particular kind of corruption.
Edmund, I think you're absolutely right — and it doesn't exclude the social reading, which is what makes the passage so combustible.
Both fires are burning at once.
And then Dickens turns, in chapter forty-seven, to Jo directly — and the register shifts completely.
This is the passage I find almost unbearably well-judged.

"He is not one of Mrs. Pardiggle's Tockahoopo Indians; he is not one of Mrs. Jellyby's lambs, being wholly unconnected with Borrioboola-Gha; he is not softened by distance and unfamiliarity; he is not a genuine foreign-grown savage; he is the ordinary home-made article."
"The ordinary home-made article."
That phrase is devastating — because it uses the language of commerce and contempt, then makes you feel the weight of it pressing down on a child.
The rhetoric of that passage is extraordinary because it mimics the language of exclusion in order to demolish it.
The anaphora — "he is not, he is not, he is not" — has the cadence of a legal document, or a charity classification form.
Dickens is inhabiting the very bureaucratic logic that excludes Jo, just long enough to make us feel its cruelty from the inside.
And then "Stand forth, Jo, in uncompromising colours" — that's almost an apostrophe, a direct address.
The narrator breaks convention to reach into the page and pull this invisible boy into visibility.
It's one of the most technically daring moments in the whole novel.
One notices that the omniscient narrator does something here that Esther never could.
Esther's voice is too interior, too personally implicated, to achieve this kind of cold sweep of irony.
The dual narration is not merely a structural curiosity — it allows Dickens to modulate moral temperature chapter by chapter.
And that leads rather naturally to the Tom-all-Alone's passage, which is among the most pointed political satire Dickens ever wrote.
"Tom only may and can, or shall and will, be reclaimed according to somebody's theory but nobody's practice."
The juridical grammar — may and can, shall and will — is a perfect parody of Parliamentary futility.
Even I, who resist the political reading at every turn, must admit that sentence is a killing blow.
Edmund admitting defeat is itself a kind of literary event.
But the comedy doesn't leave us even in the darkest passages — and chapter fifty-eight proves it.
Dickens turns to the mercers and jewellers and the librarian Sladdery managing the spread of gossip about Lady Dedlock — and it's pure farce, except that it isn't.
Sladdery says — and I think you have to enjoy the brass of this — he says:
"Our people, sir, are sheep — mere sheep. Where two or three marked ones go, all the rest follow."
He says this without any embarrassment whatsoever — this is his professional expertise, his competitive advantage.
Dickens has invented the focus group and the social media algorithm in a single paragraph.
The Sladdery passage is technically a piece of embedded monologue — reported speech that takes on the full voice of the speaker.
What's brilliant is how Dickens uses the repetition of "sir" — Sladdery is performing deference while describing manipulation.
He can wind fashionable society up like a clock — his own phrase — and he uses it with something approaching pride.
The comedy is so sharp because it requires no exaggeration — just precise observation and a perfectly calibrated deadpan.
Dickens doesn't need to tell us this is grotesque; he trusts the reader to feel it.
Johnson remarked that a man who is tired of London is tired of life.
One might say that a reader who is tired of Dickens' grotesques is tired of human nature itself.
What unites Skimpole and Sladdery is not class or politics but a failure of moral seriousness — a refusal to look clearly at the human cost of their own comfort.
Dickens makes them funny because laughter is how we first recognise the type — and then he makes sure the laughter curdles.
That, I would submit, is a very old and very serious art.
And that phrase — "laughter that curdles" — feels like exactly the right way to describe what Dickens does throughout this novel.
He never lets the comedy be merely comic, and he never lets the darkness be merely dark.
Thank you all — we'll be back shortly to turn to the question of justice, and what this novel really believes about whether it can ever be done.

segments.title: Interconnection and Entanglement: How Dickens Weaves

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — the podcast that takes Dickens' great labyrinthine novel apart, thread by thread, to see how it actually works.
I'm your host, and today we're asking one of the novel's central questions: how does Dickens hold this enormous, sprawling, many-charactered world together?
How does a story that ranges from Lincolnshire fog to a crossing-sweeper's broom, from the Lord Chancellor to a half-mad Miss Flite, cohere into something felt rather than merely catalogued?
With me to unpick that are three voices I'm delighted to have around this table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose critical eye is trained above all on craft — on how Dickens builds his effects from the sentence up.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a profound moral novel — a story about character, conscience, and the individual tested by an indifferent world.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to the text as a performer, hearing its rhythms, its comedy, its silences.
Let's begin with the novel's opening gambit — Jarndyce and Jarndyce, and what Dickens does with it as a device of connection.
What strikes me first about that opening Chancery sequence is how deliberately Dickens constructs corruption as a contagion rather than a verdict.
He doesn't say: the law is bad and these people are bad because of it.
He traces the contamination through a whole social organism — from the master with his impaling files, all the way down to the copying-clerk.
And the syntax enacts it — that great descending catalogue is itself a kind of legal document, inexorable and cumulative.
Then he arrives at what I think is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the chapter.
"Even those who have contemplated its history from the outermost circle of such evil have been insensibly tempted into a loose way of letting bad things alone to take their own bad course."
That word — insensibly — is doing everything.
Nobody chose complicity. It crept in. That's what makes it so structurally frightening — and so novelistically useful to Dickens.
Eleanor's absolutely right about the syntax — but when you read that passage aloud, what you also hear is the comedy lurking beneath the horror.
Chizzle, Mizzle, and Drizzle — Dickens just cannot help himself.
Three names that rhyme like a children's nonsense verse, dropped into the middle of this thunderous indictment.
The effect is almost operatic — a sudden comic grace note that makes the surrounding darkness darker by contrast.
And it's a connection of a different kind — Dickens is pulling the reader in with laughter even as he's implicating us in the critique.
You can't quite maintain your virtuous outrage when you're smiling at Drizzle.
Oliver's point about implication is one I'd want to press on, because I think it reaches something deeper than comic technique.
What Dickens is describing — this insensible sliding into moral inertia — is a precise account of how civilisations corrupt themselves.
Burke would have recognised it immediately. The gradual abandonment of principle, dressed as pragmatism.
But Dickens is not merely describing a broken institution — he's showing us how broken institutions reproduce broken souls.
That receiver in the cause — he has acquired money and simultaneously lost the capacity for trust.
Dickens writes: he has acquired a distrust of his own mother and a contempt for his own kind.
"He has acquired too a distrust of his own mother and a contempt for his own kind."
The word 'acquired' — used twice — is surgically precise. What one acquires through Chancery is always a corruption of what one might have been.
And this corruption, as you're all tracing it, radiates outward — which brings us to one of the novel's most celebrated structural moves.
The moment in chapter sixteen where the narrator pauses to pose a question that is almost cosmological in its reach.
Edmund, this passage has been central to your thinking about the novel's architecture — would you take us into it?
With pleasure. Because this is, to my mind, the hinge-point of the entire novel — the moment the narrator reveals his structural ambition.
Dickens has just shown us Lady Dedlock's world — her frozen grandeur, her powdered Mercury, the vast ornamental emptiness of Chesney Wold.
And now he pivots to Jo — the crossing-sweeper, who exists at the absolute nadir of this society.
And the narrator asks — not rhetorically, but genuinely, as if puzzled himself —

"What connexion can there be between the place in Lincolnshire, the house in town, the Mercury in powder, and the whereabout of Jo the outlaw with the broom, who had that distant ray of light upon him when he swept the churchyard-step?"
That phrase — a distant ray of light upon him — is the novel's moral imagination at full stretch.
Jo is not merely poor. He is illuminated. Dickens insists we see him — even before we know why we must.
That question — 'what connexion can there be' — is also a formal declaration of the novel's method.
Dickens is telling us, quite openly: this is a novel about hidden threads.
The two narrative voices — Esther's first person and the omniscient present tense — are themselves a formal enactment of that question.
Esther sees from inside her own limited experience; the omniscient narrator sees what she cannot.
Together, they triangulate the novel's world — and the reader is constantly doing the work of connection between them.
It's an extraordinarily sophisticated structure for a serialised Victorian novel — and it's hiding in plain sight.
I want to come back to Jo for a moment, because that passage becomes even more extraordinary when you hold it against Esther's voice later in the novel.
There's a passage in Esther's narration — Gridley's final words, as she recalls them — that shows the same connective logic but felt from the inside.
Gridley, dying, speaks of Miss Flite — that tiny, tragicomic figure who haunts Chancery like a ghost who hasn't noticed she's dead.
And what he says about that connection is —
"There is a tie of many suffering years between us two, and it is the only tie I ever had on earth that Chancery has not broken!"
The exclamation mark there — Dickens earns it.
Everything Chancery touches it severs — family, hope, purpose, self-belief.
But two broken people, thrown together by the same catastrophe, form the one bond it cannot reach.
Oliver has touched on something I find deeply moving in Gridley — a man consumed by righteous rage who discovers, at the last, that he is capable of tenderness.
Dickens is not, pace certain readings, simply indicting the system.
He is showing how, even within the machinery of destruction, the human spirit finds — or forges — its connexions.

Esther's narration registers it with that characteristic understated gravity — 'the shadow of that pair, one living and one dead, fell heavier on Richard's departure than the darkness of the darkest night.'
"The shadow of that pair, one living and one dead, fell heavier on Richard's departure than the darkness of the darkest night."
Esther does not dramatise her sorrow. She measures it. That is her greatness as a narrator.
And Richard himself is a case study in what happens when those connections are severed — or perhaps never properly formed.
There's a passage in chapter thirty-nine — Richard walking through Lincoln's Inn — that Edmund, you've described as one of Dickens' most chilling structural images.
Chilling is precisely the right word — though the prose is bathed in sunlight, which makes it worse.
Richard emerges from the shadow of Symond's Inn into Chancery Lane — and Dickens notes, with his habitual irony, that there happens to be sunshine today.
That parenthesis — 'for there happens to be sunshine there to-day' — is the narratorial equivalent of a raised eyebrow.
The sunshine offers no protection. Richard walks straight into the shade of the Lincoln's Inn trees.
And then the narrator delivers his terrible inventory of the Chancery-broken man.
"On the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour."
The good consuming and consumed — a chiasmus of self-destruction.
And that final question: 'why should one be different from ten thousand?' — Chancery does not permit exceptions.
What Edmund is describing — that list — is something Dickens does throughout the novel as a connective device.
The accumulating noun phrase — head, nail, eye, step, air — isn't decorative. It is diagnostic.
Dickens is cataloguing the symptoms of a known disease — and the reader recognises the disease because they've been watching it spread since chapter one.
Richard is now connected — horribly, invisibly — to every Chancery ghost who walked under those same trees before him.
That's the darkest kind of interconnection in this novel — not the web of plot, but the web of fate.
I read that passage aloud for a recording some years ago, and I remember the editor ringing me afterwards, quite shaken.
She said: 'You slowed down without being asked.' And I said: 'The prose slowed me down.'
Because that list resists rushing. Each item demands its moment. Bent head. Bitten nail. Lowering eye.
Dickens writes for a performer who knows when to give the silence its due.
And what makes it so shattering is that Richard isn't shabby yet — Dickens tells us so — but that may come.
Three words. The most economical prophecy in the novel.
That economy in the dark — and we'll find it again in one final passage I want to bring us to.
Chapter forty-eight opens with one of the most extraordinary set pieces in the novel — a moonlit panorama that sweeps across the entire country before narrowing to a single window.
Oliver, this is the kind of passage that must do something remarkable when read aloud — can you walk us through it?
It's the great 'not only' passage — and it's one of the most audacious things Dickens ever wrote, structurally speaking.
He begins with 'not only' — and then he doesn't let that syntactic breath out for nearly a page.
High roads, hill-summits, gardens, woods, the river, wharves, marshes, the sea — the moonlight touches everything, holds everything together.
He is giving us, in one sustained sentence, the connectedness of the whole world.
And then he arrives at Tulkinghorn's city — and the tone turns.

"In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn's inhabiting, where the shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them exceeding close —"
"— every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating."
A vast glass, vibrating. You could build a cathedral on that image.
That pastoral metaphor — the Chancery shepherds, the shorn sheep — is doing something almost savage.
The pastoral is supposed to be the register of innocence, of natural harmony. Dickens poisons it.
Chancery pipes that have no stop — the law that never ends, the music that never resolves.
And the image of the city as a vibrating glass — everything connected, everything resonating, everything on the edge of shattering.
That is Dickens' vision of interconnection at its most vertiginous — beauty and danger held in the same trembling frame.
I find myself wanting to resist the purely aesthetic reading here — though Eleanor makes it difficult.
The moonlight that falls on everything equally is not, I think, a metaphor for systemic injustice.
It is something more ancient — Providence, perhaps. The sense that everything in this world is seen and known, even if not yet accounted for.
Dickens was not a systematic thinker. But he was a profoundly moral one.

And what this passage tells me is that the connectedness of the novel is ultimately a moral claim — that we cannot be indifferent to one another, because we are, in ways we cannot foresee, already entwined.
Already entwined — and perhaps already implicated.
That word from earlier — insensibly — keeps echoing, doesn't it.
A vast glass, vibrating. The fog that connects rather than obscures. The question — 'what connexion can there be?' — posed not to be answered, but to be felt.
Thank you to Eleanor, Edmund, and Oliver — and to you for listening.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment — where that web of connection is tested to breaking point.
We've arrived at the place every great novel must finally bring us — its reckoning.
Bleak House ends not with triumph but with something stranger and more honest — a hush.
Lady Dedlock buried in mystery, Richard wasted and finally stilled, Chesney Wold gone silent as a held breath.
Eleanor, I want to begin with you — and with a passage I find almost unbearably beautiful.
Dickens, in the omniscient narration, turns on Lady Dedlock a series of questions — raw, unanswered, devastating.
What is he doing there, technically and emotionally?
What he's doing is something I'd call — and I don't use the word lightly — an act of structural mercy.
The omniscient narrator has spent most of the novel being knowing, almost godlike — withholding, observing, occasionally devastating.
But here, suddenly, he abandons statement and shifts entirely into questions.
Listen to what that does — it refuses to explain Lady Dedlock's inner life even as it exposes it completely.
He sets it up with this wonderful rhetorical drift —
"In search of what? Of any hand that is no more, of any hand that never was, of any touch that might have magically changed her life?"
Three times the construction circles — any hand, any hand, any touch — each one a little more heartbreaking than the last.
And then the child's footsteps — pattering, ever coming on — on — on — it's almost unbearable.
I've read that passage aloud perhaps forty times, and those dashes — on — on — on — still get me every time.
Dickens is writing for the voice there — the repetition with its tiny gaps isn't just punctuation, it's breath.
It's the sound of a child's feet that never arrive, never stop approaching.
And then the close — which is extraordinary — the narrator doesn't answer his own questions.
He simply poses the final one, cold and plain:
"Some melancholy influence is upon her, or why should so proud a lady close the doors and sit alone upon the hearth so desolate?"
That word — desolate — at the very end of the sentence, after all that pride and grandeur.
It lands like a stone dropping into still water.
I would resist the temptation — charming though it is — to read Lady Dedlock purely as a victim of circumstance.
Dickens gives her desolation — yes — but he grounds it in a choice she made: pride over love, concealment over truth.
The Ghost's Walk — that ancestral punishment for a wife who defied her husband — is not merely gothic atmosphere.
It is Dickens reminding us that moral consequences are real, that they accumulate through generations.
Burke might have said — and I think Dickens would have agreed — that the sins of the fathers, and the mothers, are not so easily buried.
Lady Dedlock ends in the mausoleum — and Chesney Wold ends in silence — not because the system destroyed her, but because she could not face the truth in time.
I don't entirely disagree — but I'd note that Dickens makes the consequences fall rather asymmetrically, doesn't he?
Hawdon dies obscure and unmourned in a squalid graveyard; Lady Dedlock dies and gets a mausoleum, a mystery, and a suppression campaign funded by a baronet.
And Dickens notices the irony with this wonderfully arch passage:

"The story goes that Sir Leicester paid some who could have spoken out to hold their peace; but it is a lame story, feebly whispering and creeping about, and any brighter spark of life it shows soon dies away."
The prose itself enacts what it describes — it feebly whispers and creeps, the syntax trailing off like a rumour losing momentum.
That is the art — the form and content becoming identical.
And then — and this is Dickens at his most sublimely deadpan — the ancestors in the mausoleum get a line.
The peachy-cheeked charmers with their skeleton throats suggest the Dedlock dead would object to Lady Dedlock's company.
And Dickens simply closes it with:
"But the dead-and-gone Dedlocks take it very calmly and have never been known to object."
After everything — the fog, the Chancery, the betrayals, the grief — Dickens will not let the aristocracy have even their posthumous snobbery.
The dead take it calmly because death, at least, is democratic.
I'll grant Oliver that — and I confess the comedy there is irresistible.
But let me turn, if I may, to Richard — because this is where Dickens is at his most morally serious, and his most heartbreaking.
Esther goes to see him near the end — he is lying on the sofa, spent, drained of colour.
And Dickens gives us this observation, so quiet it almost escapes notice:
"Now that I saw him without his seeing me, I fully saw, for the first time, how worn away he was."
For the first time — Esther has been watching Richard destroy himself through the entire novel, and only now does she truly see it.
This is the unbearable grammar of love — that we see those we love most clearly when they can no longer see us seeing them.
And then — heartbreakingly — he looked handsomer than she had seen him look for many a day.
That sentence does something structurally devastating — it holds tenderness and grief in perfect suspension.
Esther narrates it so plainly — no histrionics, no underlining — which is entirely characteristic of her voice.
But Dickens has made the plainness do all the work of the most elaborate grief.
Richard looks handsome because — and this is the novel's terrible logic — the compulsion has finally stopped consuming him.
He is at peace only because the fight has left him entirely.
When I read that passage in the recording studio, I had to stop.
Not because I was overcome — though I was — but because I realised that Dickens had set a trap.
He has spent hundreds of pages making Richard infuriating — weak, self-deceiving, wasteful of every gift.
And then, with the gentlest possible hand, he gives him back his beauty in the moment before the end.
You find yourself grieving for a man you've been frustrated with for nine hundred pages.
That is not sentiment — that is mastery.
I think that might be the finest possible note on which to close this conversation — mastery.
A novel about fog and silence and the weight of unspoken things — and Dickens clears the air at last, not with resolution, but with grace.
Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you for the intelligence and the feeling you've brought to every page of this.
Bleak House, in the end, refuses bleakness — and that refusal is earned on every sentence.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

c1:p4.text:
Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire
too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which
this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds
this day in the sight of heaven and earth.
c1:p4.summary: The fog and mud perfectly match the corrupt, floundering condition of the High Court of Chancery, which the narrator condemns as pestilent and sinful.
c1:p4.best_quote: Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds this day in the sight of heaven and earth.

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.
c1:p5.best_quote: This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance.

c17:p0.text:
Richard very often came to see us while we remained in London (though
he soon failed in his letter-writing), and with his quick abilities,
his good spirits, his good temper, his gaiety and freshness, was
always delightful. But though I liked him more and more the better I
knew him, I still felt more and more how much it was to be regretted
that he had been educated in no habits of application and
concentration. The system which had addressed him in exactly the same
manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in
character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks,
always with fair credit and often with distinction, but in a fitful,
dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities
in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train. They
were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously
won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were
very bad masters. If they had been under Richard’s direction, they
would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction,
they became his enemies.
c17:p0.summary: Esther reflects on Richard's natural talents being undermined by his lack of discipline, a problem rooted in an educational system that addresses all students identically rather than according to individual capacity.
c17:p0.best_quote: They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.

c37:p72.text:
Poor dear Richard! He had indeed been thinking about it a good deal.
His face, his voice, his manner, all showed that too plainly.
c37:p72.summary: Richard declares his absolute commitment to resolving the Chancery suit, his intensity revealing his obsession.
c37:p72.best_quote: It can't last for ever. I am young and earnest, and energy and determination have done wonders many a time. Others have only half thrown themselves into it. I devote myself to it. I make it the object of my life.

c39:p44.text:
Yet the time is so short since his depreciation began that as he
saunters away, reluctant to leave the spot for some long months
together, though he hates it, Richard himself may feel his own case
as if it were a startling one. While his heart is heavy with
corroding care, suspense, distrust, and doubt, it may have room for
some sorrowful wonder when he recalls how different his first visit
there, how different he, how different all the colours of his mind.
But injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being
defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat;
from the impalpable suit which no man alive can understand, the time
for that being long gone by, it has become a gloomy relief to turn to
the palpable figure of the friend who would have saved him from this
ruin and make HIM his enemy. Richard has told Vholes the truth. Is he
in a hardened or a softened mood, he still lays his injuries equally
at that door; he was thwarted, in that quarter, of a set purpose, and
that purpose could only originate in the one subject that is
resolving his existence into itself; besides, it is a justification
to him in his own eyes to have an embodied antagonist and oppressor.
c39:p44.summary: The narrator analyzes how Richard's corruption has progressed: unable to combat the abstract suit, he has seized upon Jarndyce as a concrete enemy and embodiment of all his injuries, justifying himself with the logic of having an enemy.
c39:p44.best_quote: injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat

c51:p27.text:
“Nor I,” said Richard moodily. “Who ever did?” He brightened again in
a moment and said with his natural openness, “Woodcourt, I should be
sorry to be misunderstood by you, even if I gained by it in your
estimation. You must know that I have done no good this long time. I
have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of
nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out
of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not,
though I dare say you will soon hear, if you have not already heard,
a very different opinion. To make short of a long story, I am afraid
I have wanted an object; but I have an object now—or it has me—and
it is too late to discuss it. Take me as I am, and make the best of
me.”
c51:p27.summary: Richard confesses to Woodcourt that he has accomplished nothing, lacks purpose, and feels trapped by fate and the Chancery suit, yet demands acceptance without judgment.
c51:p27.best_quote: I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not.

c51:p59.text:
His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his
despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in
its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so
conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched
me to the heart. But the commentary upon it now indelibly written in
his handsome face made it far more distressing than it used to be. I
say indelibly, for I felt persuaded that if the fatal cause could
have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in
that same hour, the traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach,
and disappointment it had occasioned him would have remained upon his
features to the hour of his death.
c51:p59.summary: Esther reflects deeply on the tragedy of Richard's forced optimism, which has worn itself into his face as permanent marks of anxiety and self-reproach that will outlast any resolution of the suit.
c51:p59.best_quote: His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched me to the heart.

c60:p96.text:
We sat down to dinner, and I had an opportunity of observing Richard,
anxiously. I was not disturbed by Mr. Vholes (who took off his gloves
to dine), though he sat opposite to me at the small table, for I
doubt if, looking up at all, he once removed his eyes from his host’s
face. I found Richard thin and languid, slovenly in his dress,
abstracted in his manner, forcing his spirits now and then, and at
other intervals relapsing into a dull thoughtfulness. About his large
bright eyes that used to be so merry there was a wanness and a
restlessness that changed them altogether. I cannot use the
expression that he looked old. There is a ruin of youth which is not
like age, and into such a ruin Richard’s youth and youthful beauty
had all fallen away.
c60:p96.summary: Esther observes Richard's alarming physical decline: he is thin, languid, slovenly, abstracted, with dull eyes instead of his old merry brightness, embodying a tragic ruin of youth.
c60:p96.best_quote: There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away.

c16:p11.text:
It must be a strange state to be like Jo! To shuffle through the
streets, unfamiliar with the shapes, and in utter darkness as to the
meaning, of those mysterious symbols, so abundant over the shops, and
at the corners of streets, and on the doors, and in the windows! To
see people read, and to see people write, and to see the postmen
deliver letters, and not to have the least idea of all that
language—to be, to every scrap of it, stone blind and dumb! It must
be very puzzling to see the good company going to the churches on
Sundays, with their books in their hands, and to think (for perhaps
Jo DOES think at odd times) what does it all mean, and if it means
anything to anybody, how comes it that it means nothing to me? To be
hustled, and jostled, and moved on; and really to feel that it would
appear to be perfectly true that I have no business here, or there,
or anywhere; and yet to be perplexed by the consideration that I AM
here somehow, too, and everybody overlooked me until I became the
creature that I am! It must be a strange state, not merely to be told
that I am scarcely human (as in the case of my offering myself for a
witness), but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life! To see the
horses, dogs, and cattle go by me and to know that in ignorance I
belong to them and not to the superior beings in my shape, whose
delicacy I offend! Jo’s ideas of a criminal trial, or a judge, or a
bishop, or a government, or that inestimable jewel to him (if he only
knew it) the Constitution, should be strange! His whole material and
immaterial life is wonderfully strange; his death, the strangest
thing of all.
c16:p11.summary: The narrator powerfully explores Jo's alienation from literate society, meaning-making, and human dignity, showing how systemic exclusion has made him feel less than human.
c16:p11.best_quote: It must be a strange state, not merely to be told that I am scarcely human (as in the case of my offering myself for a witness), but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life!

c11:p100.text:
Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who “can’t
exactly say” what will be done to him in greater hands than men’s,
thou art not quite in outer darkness. There is something like a
distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: “He wos wery
good to me, he wos!”
c11:p100.summary: The narrator directly addresses Jo, acknowledging his legal rejection but affirming that his love for the dead man is a form of grace and light.
c11:p100.best_quote: There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'

c46:p40.text:
“Yes, I see you once afore at the inkwhich,” whimpers Jo. “What of
that? Can’t you never let such an unfortnet as me alone? An’t I
unfortnet enough for you yet? How unfortnet do you want me fur to be?
I’ve been a-chivied and a-chivied, fust by one on you and nixt by
another on you, till I’m worritted to skins and bones. The inkwhich
warn’t MY fault. I done nothink. He wos wery good to me, he wos; he
wos the only one I knowed to speak to, as ever come across my
crossing. It ain’t wery likely I should want him to be inkwhiched. I
only wish I wos, myself. I don’t know why I don’t go and make a hole
in the water, I’m sure I don’t.”
c46:p40.summary: Jo speaks in dialect of his persecution by the legal system and others, mentioning the coroner's inquest and expressing suicidal despair.
c46:p40.best_quote: I've been a-chivied and a-chivied, fust by one on you and nixt by another on you, till I'm worritted to skins and bones.

c19:p54.text:
Do you hear, Jo? It is nothing to you or to any one else that the
great lights of the parliamentary sky have failed for some few years
in this business to set you the example of moving on. The one grand
recipe remains for you—the profound philosophical prescription—the
be-all and the end-all of your strange existence upon earth. Move on!
You are by no means to move off, Jo, for the great lights can’t at
all agree about that. Move on!
c19:p54.summary: The narrator directly addresses Jo in biting language, condemning Parliament and lawmakers for failing to solve vagrancy while imposing 'move on' orders on the poor.
c19:p54.best_quote: Do you hear, Jo? It is nothing to you or to any one else that the great lights of the parliamentary sky have failed for some few years in this business to set you the example of moving on. The one grand recipe remains for you—the profound philosophical prescription—the be-all and the end-all of your strange existence upon earth. Move on!

c47:p139.text:
Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right
reverends and wrong reverends of every order. Dead, men and women,
born with heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around
us every day.
c47:p139.summary: The narrator directly addresses the Crown, nobility, clergy, and all compassionate people, condemning their collective indifference to deaths like Jo's occurring daily among the poor.
c47:p139.best_quote: Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day.

c2:p2.text:
My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”
c2:p2.summary: Lady Dedlock returns to her Lincolnshire estate before departing for Paris, where the landscape is depicted as relentlessly dreary and sodden; her observation of a family scene at a keeper's lodge disrupts her usual composure.
c2:p2.best_quote: The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink

c12:p116.text:
Mr. Tulkinghorn does so with deference and holds it open while she
passes out. She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner
and insolent grace. They meet again at dinner—again, next
day—again, for many days in succession. Lady Dedlock is always the
same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable
to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine. Mr.
